authorities.name: Localism Act 2011, s.1(1) - general power of competence
authorities.date_note: Enactment year. The text verified this session is the current in-force (revised) version, recently extended by the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 (in force April/June 2026) to combined authorities, CCAs, English National Park authorities, and the Broads Authority - confirmed live, not assumed. The page also flags separate pending changes (2016 c.22 substitutions to s.158) not yet applied, unrelated to s.1(1)'s own text.
authorities.proposition: A principal local authority has the power to do anything an individual generally may do, exercisable in any way and for any purpose (commercial or non-commercial), unless expressly limited elsewhere - the 'general power of competence' that superseded the older, narrower ultra vires approach to what a local authority could lawfully do.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time - both fetches consistent on s.1(1)'s exact text and the live 2026 extension.

authorities.name: R (GS) v London Borough of Camden
authorities.court: High Court (Queen's Bench Division, Administrative Court)
authorities.proposition: A claimant who did not qualify for accommodation under the Care Act 2014 (an accommodation need alone, without a qualifying care-and-support need, does not trigger that Act's duty) could nonetheless require the local authority to provide accommodation using its discretionary s.1 Localism Act 2011 general power - because HRA 1998 s.6 makes it unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with a Convention right, a council cannot lawfully decline to use an available discretionary power where declining would expose the claimant to a real risk of Article 3/8 ECHR-engaging harm. The discretionary power becomes, in that situation, an enforceable duty.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly from Find Case Law this session, independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time - both fetches consistent on paragraph 76's duty-conversion holding. Cross-checked against Nearly Legal and Field Court Chambers' independent case commentary. BAILII returned HTTP 403 on a direct check and was not used - not needed here since Find Case Law covers this post-2009 case directly.

edges.verified_via: R (GS) v London Borough of Camden [2016] EWHC 1762 (Admin), paras 62 and 76, fetched directly from Find Case Law and independently re-confirmed: applies s.1's general power, converting it into a duty via HRA 1998 s.6 where declining to act would breach Convention rights.

what_this_is_not: Two verified nodes covering one narrow point: a discretionary general power converted into an enforceable duty via the Human Rights Act. Does not cover local authority finance/council tax, the fiduciary duty to taxpayers, planning functions, procurement, judicial review procedure specific to local authorities, or any other Local Government Law subject - all remain unbuilt.
